sections.body_md:
A set is bounded when some ball, of finite radius, contains it. Equivalently, the distances from the origin to its points have a finite upper bound. Boundedness alone does not keep limit points. Closedness alone does not prevent the set from running off to infinity.

In \(\mathbb{R}^n\) the two properties together are compactness. This is the Heine-Borel theorem: a subset of Euclidean space is compact exactly when it is closed and bounded. A closed ball, a sphere, a closed rectangle, and any finite set are compact. An open ball is bounded and not closed. A line, a closed half-space, and the integers are closed and unbounded.

One reason to care is attainment. A continuous real-valued function on a nonempty compact set reaches its minimum and its maximum. Drop either closedness or boundedness and a continuous function can have an infimum it never reaches.

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md:
\(S\) is bounded when there exist a center \(c\) and a radius \(R < \infty\) with \(S \subset \overline{B}(c, R)\). In \(\mathbb{R}^n\),
\[
S \text{ is compact} \iff S \text{ is closed and bounded}.
\]
A continuous \(f\) on a nonempty compact \(S\) attains \(\min_S f\) and \(\max_S f\). A closed subset of a compact set is compact. A finite union of compact sets is compact. The continuous image of a compact set is compact.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md:
The rectangle \([0, 8] \times [0, 15]\) contains its boundary, so it is closed. Its farthest point from the origin is the corner \((8, 15)\), and
\[
\sqrt{8^2 + 15^2} = \sqrt{64 + 225} = \sqrt{289} = 17.
\]
The corner distance is 17, so the rectangle sits in the closed ball of radius 17 and is bounded. It is compact.

The open rectangle \((0, 8) \times (0, 15)\) is still bounded by that same ball. It misses the corner and the edges, so it is not closed and not compact. A continuous function on the open rectangle can approach a value on the missing edge and never reach it.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md: Bounded does not imply compact. The open unit disk is the counterexample, and so is \(\{1/n: n = 1, 2, \ldots\}\), which is bounded and misses its limit 0. Closed does not imply compact: the integers are closed in \(\mathbb{R}\) and unbounded. In infinite-dimensional spaces, closed and bounded is no longer enough, so the Euclidean statement should not be copied into a space of functions. A finite set is compact even when the points are far apart. The radius only has to be large enough to cover them.

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: Existence of a minimizer is the payoff. On a nonempty compact feasible set, a continuous objective attains its minimum. On an unbounded set the same conclusion needs a coercivity argument, often read off sublevel sets. Classifying stationary points still does not by itself produce a minimizer when the domain fails to be compact. The closed-and-bounded test is the first check.
